jurisdiction: United States — state layer (all 50 states + District of Columbia). Federal/EU/India layers excluded by lane.
headline: Model B (buy coins -> stake player-v-player -> redeem for cash or prizes) is unlawful as designed, and no commercially viable licensed path exists: about ten states criminalise wagering on contests of SKILL by statute or judicial construction regardless of the skill/chance debate (AZ, AR, CA, DE, FL, IL, LA, NV, SC, SD, plus TN and WA through near-any-chance and material-element tests) — MONTANA IS REMOVED FROM THAT LIST, the statute the brief cited for it does not say what the brief said; and roughly TEN states enacted express dual-currency 'online sweepstakes' prohibitions in 2025-26 that reach payment processors, geolocation vendors and media affiliates as well as the operator (CA, CT, IN, LA, ME, MT, NJ, NY, OK, TN), with TWO MORE (IA, NV) granting regulators open-ended enforcement authority rather than defining the offence — a materially different compliance question. Licensure is not unavailable in principle: Nevada NRS 463.160 licenses any game played for money with no skill/chance distinction, and New Jersey's DGE licenses esports event wagering. The accurate statement is that NO STATE HAS AN OFF-THE-SHELF LICENCE CATEGORY THAT FITS A PEER-TO-PEER MOBILE TRIVIA APP AT VIABLE COST OR LEAD TIME. Model C (fixed, pre-announced, operator-funded prize pool, neutral operator, no randomisation on the paid path) is the only real-money design with a defensible state-law story, and it still needs geofencing of roughly eleven states plus a per-state opinion. Models A and D are lawful subject to three things the original brief under-weighted: the Washington/New York 'privilege of playing' trap, unclaimed-property duties on stored coin balances, and automatic-renewal law.

modelVerdicts.verdict: lawful — subject to two structural traps and one newly added obligation
modelVerdicts.reasoning: Closed-loop coins that buy cosmetics or entries at a fixed price and never convert to money or a prize of value fail the PRIZE element of the consideration/chance/prize test in every state, so no state gambling statute is engaged. TWO STATE-SPECIFIC TRAPS. (1) WASHINGTON: RCW 9.46.0285 defines 'thing of value' to include 'any form of credit or promise ... involving extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge', and in Kater v. Churchill Downs Inc., 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 28 Mar 2018) the Ninth Circuit held virtual casino chips were a 'thing of value' precisely because without them a user cannot play. Purchased coins that are STAKED and can be LOST therefore satisfy both the consideration and prize elements in Washington with zero cash-out. (2) NEW YORK: the identical 'extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge' formula appears at N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(6) ('Something of value') — CORRECTED: the brief cited this to s.225.00(1), which is wrong; s.225.00(1) is 'Contest of chance' (the material-degree test) and s.225.00(2) is 'Gambling'. Verified subdivision-by-subdivision at nysenate.gov on 14 Sep 2026. The substantive New York analysis survives the renumbering unchanged. So Model A is lawful ONLY in the strict form defined — coins bought at a fixed price and spent at a fixed price, NEVER risked on an uncertain outcome. The moment purchased coins are staked in a duel the analysis moves to Model B territory in WA and NY regardless of cash-out. FACT//DUEL today stakes its demo coins; keep purchased coins structurally separate from any staking mechanic. [AUDIT ADDITION] Residual state exposure is NOT only in-app-purchase disclosure and minors. Unredeemed purchased-coin balances are stored value, and several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as ABANDONED PROPERTY with reporting and remittance duties to the state treasurer. Model A accumulates exactly that balance. Specific state thresholds, dormancy periods and whether closed-loop game currency is exempt in a given state are UNVERIFIED — this needs an unclaimed-property review alongside the gambling review. [AUDIT ADDITION] Age of majority is not 18 in every state: Alabama and Nebraska set it at 19 and Mississippi at 21, which affects the enforceability of the purchase contract and of the arbitration clause against an 18-year-old in those three states (UNVERIFIED as to current statutory cites).

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Consideration (real money for coins) plus prize (cash or prizes of value) is present in all 51 jurisdictions; the only live question is chance, and for Model B that question does not save the design. THREE INDEPENDENT KILL-SHOTS. (1) STATUTES THAT REACH SKILL WAGERING EXPRESSLY, so the trivia-is-skill argument is irrelevant: Arizona A.R.S. s.13-3301(4) (gambling includes risking value for benefit from 'a game or contest of chance OR SKILL'); California Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) (any bet 'upon the result ... of any trial ... or contest ... of skill, speed or power of endurance of person or animal, OR BETWEEN PERSONS'); Florida Stat. s.849.14 ('Unlawful to bet on result of trial or contest of skill'); Delaware 11 Del. C. s.1403 (registering 'bets or wagers upon the result of any trial or contest of skill, speed or power of endurance'); Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) (playing 'a game of chance OR SKILL for money'); Louisiana R.S. 14:90 (no chance element at all — 'any game, contest, lottery, or contrivance whereby a person risks the loss of anything of value in order to realize a profit'); Nevada NRS 463.0152 ('gambling game' is any game played 'for money ... or any representative of value', no skill/chance distinction); South Dakota SDCL s.22-25A-1 ('bet or wager' by reference to 'the result of a race, contest, or game', no chance element); South Carolina S.C. Code s.16-19-40 as construed in Town of Mt. Pleasant v. Chimento (S.C. 2012) (reaches games even where skill predominates); Arkansas Code s.5-66-104 (any device 'at which any money or property may be won or lost'). CORRECTED: MONTANA IS REMOVED from this list. The brief's claim that Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 defines a lawful 'contest of skill' as one where 'the contestant is not required to pay anything of value ... to participate' is withdrawn. Verified at mca.legmt.gov on 14 Sep 2026: s.23-5-110 is titled 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' and is a legislative-findings and licensing-privilege section with no definition of 'contest of skill' and no paid-entry disqualifier; the definitions section s.23-5-112 defines 44 terms and 'contest of skill' is not among them, and its gambling definition at s.23-5-112(14)(a) is chance-based ('a gain that is contingent in whole or in part upon lot, chance, or the operation of a gambling device or gambling enterprise'), which cuts AGAINST the brief's original reading. Montana's real Model B exposure is S.B. 555, not a skill-wagering statute. (2) CHANCE TESTS THAT CATCH A RANDOMISED TRIVIA DRAW ANYWAY: Tennessee Code s.39-17-501(1) ('to any degree contingent on chance'); Washington, New York, Alabama, Kentucky, Missouri, Ohio and Oregon apply a material-element test ('depends in a material degree upon an element of chance, notwithstanding that skill of the contestants may also be a factor' — in New York that is Penal Law s.225.00(1), CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(2)). Randomised question selection, a 5-second timer against an unseen opponent, and matchmaking variance are all chance inputs a prosecutor will point at. (3) EXPRESS 2025-26 DUAL-CURRENCY BANS that criminalise the sweepstakes-casino structure and extend liability to payment processors, geolocation vendors, media affiliates and platform suppliers. CORRECTED COUNT: roughly TEN express bans, not twelve — California Penal Code s.337o (AB 831, signed 11 Oct 2025, Ch. 623, eff. 1 Jan 2026, misdemeanour, $1,000-$25,000 per violation; independently confirmed); New York Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912 (S5935A, Ch. 605 of 2025, signed 5 Dec 2025, $10,000-$100,000 per violation; independently confirmed); Oklahoma S.B. 1589 (vetoed 7 May 2026, overridden 14 May 2026, Class C2 felony, eff. 1 Nov 2026; independently confirmed); Connecticut P.A. 25-112 / S.B. 1235 (eff. 1 Oct 2025, Class D felony); Montana S.B. 555 (eff. 1 Oct 2025); plus five whose enactment particulars are UNVERIFIED and must be confirmed before they go in a launch timeline — New Jersey A5447 (text confirmed to exist and to carry $100,000/$250,000 civil penalties, but enactment and the '15 Aug 2025' signing date NOT confirmed), Indiana H.B. 1052 / P.L. 153-2026, Maine L.D. 2007, Tennessee S.B. 2136, Louisiana H.B. 53 (Act 48) and H.B. 883 (Act 182). IOWA AND NEVADA ARE NOT EXPRESS DUAL-CURRENCY BANS and must not be counted as such: Iowa S.F. 2289 is a broad enforcement grant that does not define dual-currency systems or create a new offence, and Nevada S.B. 256 added enforcement tools against unlicensed online operators. In IA and NV the compliance question turns on REGULATOR DISCRETION, not on a statutory definition the founder can read against the product — which is worse to plan around, not better. Most of these bans require the game to 'simulate casino-style gambling', which a trivia duel arguably does not, but that gap is narrow, untested, and California s.337a(a)(6) and Florida s.849.14 close it independently. ON LICENSURE — CORRECTED: it is NOT true that no state licenses this. Nevada NRS 463.0152 defines a gambling game with no skill/chance distinction and NRS 463.160 licenses exactly that; New Jersey's DGE licenses esports event wagering. Those are licensed paths. The accurate claim is that no state has an off-the-shelf licence category that fits a peer-to-peer mobile trivia app at commercially viable cost and lead time — a Nevada non-restricted licence is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar suitability process. [AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL GAMING COMPACTS are a separate state-layer risk the brief never mentioned. Exclusivity provisions in California, Florida, Oklahoma and Connecticut give tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming, and tribal objection has killed products with a clean reading of the criminal code. Specific compact provisions UNVERIFIED. [AUDIT ADDITION] PLAYER-SIDE VERSUS OPERATOR-SIDE LIABILITY: several of these statutes reach the person who plays or bets, not only the house — 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('plays a game of chance or skill for money') and Cal. Penal Code s.337a (which reaches making and ACCEPTING a bet) among them. Geofencing protects the company from the operator-side offence; it does not retroactively protect a user who played from a prohibited state, and that drives terms-of-service drafting, refund posture, and whether you owe a user their balance back. Scope of player-side liability per state: UNVERIFIED. Verdict: unlawful.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A paid-entry contest of knowledge with a FIXED prize pool announced in advance, funded by the operator and NOT dependent on the number of entrants, is the strongest real-money structure available — but it is lawful in a large majority of states and flatly unlawful in a hard core, so the honest single-word answer at the 51-jurisdiction level is unsettled. THE CASE FOR IT: most states apply the dominant-factor (predominance) test, under which a contest of general knowledge is a skill contest; and many state gambling definitions carry a model-penal-code exclusion for 'bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' (verified verbatim in Connecticut, Conn. Gen. Stat. s.53-278a). ON WHITE v. CUOMO — MATERIALLY CORRECTED. The brief called White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (N.Y. 2022) 'the best authority in the country' and told the founder to 'build to that sentence'. That overstates it in three ways and the overstatement is dangerous. (i) It was a holding on Article I s.9 of the NEW YORK CONSTITUTION only, and has NO precedential force in the other 50 jurisdictions. (ii) The contests at issue were interactive fantasy sports that the legislature had AFFIRMATIVELY AUTHORIZED in Racing Law article 14 and expressly exempted from Penal Law article 225; the court's reasoning was that ample support existed for the legislature's determination that the article 14 contests were lawful skill-based competitions. It does NOT hold that an UNAUTHORIZED paid-entry trivia contest escapes the material-degree contest-of-chance test at Penal Law s.225.00(1). A founder who builds to the sentence has satisfied a constitutional test, not the penal code. (iii) The '4-3' vote split is UNVERIFIED — a secondary source (Gibson Dunn) describes a DiFiore majority with a Wilson dissent joined by two judges, which is consistent with 4-3 but is not the opinion. Do not state the split. What survives, and it is still worth having: the three design attributes the New York Court of Appeals treated as characteristic of lawful skill competition — SUBSTANTIAL PLAYER INFLUENCE, PREDETERMINED FIXED PRIZES, NEUTRAL OPERATOR — are a sound design target, and Model C satisfies them where Model B does not. Treat it as a design heuristic with New York constitutional support, not as clearance. THE CASE AGAINST IT: the skill-wagering statutes listed under Model B do not care whether the prize is fixed — Arizona (skill contests are gambling by definition; the s.13-3311 'amusement gambling intellectual contest' registration route works only for merchandise prizes under $10 with no price increment, so it is useless for cash prizes), Delaware (Del. Const. art. II s.17 plus 11 Del. C. s.1403), Florida s.849.14, Louisiana R.S. 14:90 (as-a-business, no chance element), South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Washington (RCW 9.46.240 makes transmitting gambling information over the internet a CLASS C FELONY). MONTANA MOVES from 'absolute geofence' to UNRESOLVED for Model C: with s.23-5-110 withdrawn, the operative definition is the chance-based s.23-5-112(14)(a), under which an operator-funded fixed-prize knowledge contest with randomisation stripped out has an argument — but S.B. 555 still bars any dual-currency structure and a Montana opinion is required. Nevada is a licence state whose only fitting licence is commercially out of reach. Arkansas is prohibited unless the contest qualifies as a 'paid esports tournament' under Ark. Code ss.23-118-102/103 (eff. 31 Jul 2023) — a trivia app probably does not. WHAT MAKES IT WORKABLE: geofence AZ, AR, DE, FL, LA, NV, SC, SD, TN, WA plus CT and IL on a conservative read, and MT until a Montana opinion clears it; make the prize pool fixed, announced, operator-funded and entrant-count-independent; take no rake from a player-funded pot; keep the operator a non-participant; strip randomisation out of the paid path. Then register where prize-promotion registration bites (NY GBL s.369-e over $5,000; FL Stat. s.849.094 over $5,000; RI over $500 retail). [AUDIT ADDITION] THE FREE-ENTRY / AMOE ALTERNATIVE WAS NEVER EVALUATED and it is the standard industry structure: a genuine alternative method of entry (free postal or in-app entry of equal dignity, no purchase necessary, equal odds and equal prize eligibility) removes the CONSIDERATION element and, in states whose bar is consideration-based rather than an express skill-wagering prohibition, can open jurisdictions that are closed to paid entry. It does NOT help in Arizona, Florida, Delaware, South Dakota or Louisiana, whose statutes do not turn on consideration in that way, and — decisively — the entire 2025-26 legislative wave catalogued here IS THE LEGISLATIVE RESPONSE TO EXACTLY THIS STRUCTURE: the dual-currency sweepstakes bans exist because operators used an AMOE to claim they were not gambling. So AMOE is a live option for a PROMOTIONAL contest but is the single most legislatively targeted design in the country right now. Strategy-space completeness requires costing it; adopting it requires a per-state opinion. UNVERIFIED as to which states it actually opens. Needs a per-state opinion from gaming counsel before launch.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A recurring fee for features or cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value engages no state gambling statute in any of the 51 jurisdictions — there is no prize, and in most states there is no risk of loss on an uncertain outcome either. The state-layer burden is consumer protection, not gaming, and it is real: roughly 25 states have automatic-renewal laws and the 2025-26 wave tightened them. California's Automatic Renewal Law (Bus. & Prof. Code s.17600 et seq.) as amended by A.B. 2863 (signed 24 Sep 2024, eff. 1 Jul 2025) requires express affirmative consent, covers free-to-pay conversions, requires advance notice of fee changes 7-30 days out, and mandates SAME-MEDIUM cancellation. Virginia's ARL amendments take effect 1 Jul 2026 and require an online cancel path at least as easy as sign-up (bill number UNVERIFIED). New York City's click-to-cancel rule takes effect 1 Oct 2026 for subscriptions offered to NYC consumers (rule citation UNVERIFIED). If the subscription is sold through Apple or Google, their billing and cancellation flows satisfy most of the mechanics, but the disclosure obligations still sit on the publisher. One design caution: do not let a subscription confer coins that are then STAKED — that re-imports the Model A/B analysis. [AUDIT ADDITION] Two additions. (1) UNCLAIMED PROPERTY: a subscription that accrues a coin or credit balance creates stored value, and several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as abandoned property with reporting and remittance duties. Thresholds, dormancy periods and closed-loop exemptions per state: UNVERIFIED. (2) AGE OF MAJORITY IS NOT 18 EVERYWHERE — Alabama and Nebraska 19, Mississippi 21 — which bears on whether the subscription contract and its arbitration clause bind an 18-to-20-year-old in those states (statutory cites UNVERIFIED).

checklist.cost: Engineering + geolocation vendor fee (UNVERIFIED — gaming-grade geolocation vendors do not publish rates). Note the vendor itself takes on liability in CA, NY and OK, which is a pricing and willingness-to-onboard factor.
checklist.leadTime: Must be live before the first paid transaction
checklist.prerequisite: Server-authoritative accounts with a verified state of residence; FACT//DUEL is currently local-only IndexedDB with no accounts, so accounts are a hard prerequisite
checklist.notes: This is the industry-standard block list. Skillz's published legal terms restrict real-prize play in AZ, AR, CT, DE, LA, MT, SC, SD, TN (9) and additionally ME and IN where playing cards are involved. Add NV (licence state, no commercially viable licence), FL (Fla. Stat. s.849.14) and WA (RCW 9.46.240, Class C felony) for a defensible 12. CORRECTED: MONTANA STAYS ON THIS LIST but for a different reason than the brief gave. Montana is NOT a skill-wagering-statute state — Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 is 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' and defines nothing (verified at mca.legmt.gov, 14 Sep 2026), and s.23-5-112 contains no 'contest of skill' definition; Montana's gambling definition at s.23-5-112(14)(a) is chance-based. Montana is on the list because of S.B. 555 (dual-currency ban, eff. 1 Oct 2025). For Model C specifically, Montana is now UNRESOLVED rather than absolutely barred and a Montana opinion could remove it. [AUDIT ADDITION] Geofencing protects the OPERATOR from the operator-side offence. It does not by itself resolve PLAYER-SIDE liability under statutes that reach the person who plays (720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1); Cal. Penal Code s.337a reaches accepting AND making a bet) — build the terms of service and the refund/return-of-balance posture on that assumption.

checklist.item: Geofence or disable dual-currency redemption in the states with 2025-26 online-sweepstakes legislation. CORRECTED: this is TEN states with an EXPRESS DUAL-CURRENCY PROHIBITION (CA, CT, IN, LA, ME, MT, NJ, NY, OK, TN) plus TWO with an OPEN-ENDED ENFORCEMENT-AUTHORITY GRANT and no statutory dual-currency definition (IA, NV). The brief counted all twelve as bans; they are not the same compliance question. Several also make YOUR VENDORS liable.

checklist.cost: Statutory penalties if breached: CA $1,000-$25,000/violation plus up to 1 yr (confirmed); NY $10,000-$100,000/violation (confirmed); OK Class C2 felony (confirmed); CT Class D felony; NJ $100,000 first offence / $250,000 subsequent (text confirmed, enactment UNVERIFIED); IN civil to $100,000 (UNVERIFIED); LA to $100,000 plus racketeering (UNVERIFIED).

[AUDIT ADDITION] EFFECTIVE-DATE SEQUENCING: OKLAHOMA S.B. 1589 takes effect 1 NOV 2026 and is the ONLY listed prohibition not yet operative today. Dates: NY 5 Dec 2025 (confirmed); CA 1 Jan 2026 (confirmed); CT and MT 1 Oct 2025; OK 1 Nov 2026 (confirmed, veto overridden 14 May 2026). NJ '15 Aug 2025', IN and IA '1 Jul 2026', ME 'Jul 2026', TN '22 May 2026' and LA '1 Aug 2026' are all UNVERIFIED signing/effect dates — [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] keep them as working assumptions only and confirm from the enrolled bills before they enter a launch plan. checklist.prerequisite: Legal determination of whether FACT//DUEL 'simulates casino-style gambling' — most of the ten express bans require that element and a trivia duel arguably does not, but CA Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) and FL s.849.14 catch skill wagering independently. In IOWA and NEVADA there is no such definitional element to argue against: the question is whether the Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission or the Nevada Gaming Control Board decides to act, which cannot be resolved by reading the statute and is therefore HARDER, not easier, to plan around.

Wag. & Breeding L. s.912 and OK S.B. 1589 all extend liability to payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, content suppliers and MEDIA AFFILIATES who knowingly support the platform. That means your Stripe/Adyen equivalent, your geolocation vendor and your affiliate marketers can be prosecuted — in practice they will refuse to onboard you.

All figures are aggregated from licensing-consultancy and law-firm sources, NOT from state fee schedules — re-price from current NMLS state-specific requirements before budgeting.

checklist.notes: CORRECTED, and this matters more than any other line in the checklist. Most state MTL regimes — and the CSBS MTMA definition this brief relies on elsewhere — turn on RECEIVING MONEY FOR TRANSMISSION TO ANOTHER PERSON. An operator that takes deposits and pays its OWN prize obligations out of its OWN funds is frequently not transmitting to a third party and may fall outside the definition entirely in many states. That is precisely MODEL C: operator-funded, fixed, entrant-count-independent prizes. MODEL B — where you hold one player's stake for payment to another player — squarely raises money transmission. The brief's flat '49 states plus DC, the single largest cost and time line item in the whole plan' materially OVERSTATES the burden for the very design it recommends. Correct posture: assume a full 49-state-plus-DC programme for Model B (multi-year, seven-figure, effectively disqualifying for a startup); for Model C, get a money-transmission opinion on the transmission-to-another-person question FIRST, because the answer may be that no licence is required at all. Which states depart from the transmission-to-another-person formulation is UNVERIFIED and is the specific question to put to counsel.

checklist.item: AVOID the MTL problem structurally: never take custody of player funds. Route deposits and payouts through a licensed payment provider or sponsor bank so that the provider, not you, is the money transmitter.

checklist.notes: The operative conclusion does not depend on the count and should be stated without false precision: PLAN FOR 49 APPLICATIONS, NOT ONE. CSBS says MTMA states cover the large majority of reported money transmission activity, but Cooley is explicit that 'managing compliance with money transmission laws generally remains a state-by-state proposition' — states added bespoke provisions, excluded payroll processors, and diverged on bonds (Maine set a fixed bond instead of the model formula). Massachusetts (eff. 1 Jan 2026) and Virginia (eff. 1 Jul 2026) are reported adopters; the roster and the total are UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: Restructure the paid product to Model C: fixed prize pool, announced BEFORE entries open, funded by the operator, NOT scaled to entrant count, with the operator as a neutral non-participant taking no rake from a player-funded pot.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.cost: Operator-funded prize liability (a real P&L cost, unlike a rake)
checklist.prerequisite: Kill player-v-player escrow entirely on the paid path
checklist.notes: This tracks the design attributes the New York Court of Appeals treated as characteristic of lawful skill competition in White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (2022): 'skill-based competitions in which participants who exercise substantial influence over the outcome of the contest are awarded predetermined fixed prizes by a neutral operator'. CORRECTED — DO NOT TREAT THIS AS CLEARANCE. White v. Cuomo was decided under Article I s.9 of the NEW YORK CONSTITUTION, about interactive fantasy sports that the legislature had affirmatively authorized in Racing Law article 14 AND expressly exempted from Penal Law article 225. It has no precedential force outside New York, and it does NOT hold that an unauthorized paid-entry trivia contest escapes the material-degree contest-of-chance test at N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1). The brief's instruction to 'build to that sentence' would let a founder conclude New York is cleared by design compliance alone. It is not. Use the three attributes as a design target; get a New York opinion separately. The reported 4-3 vote split is UNVERIFIED — do not cite it. An entrant-count-dependent pot converts the structure back into a wager and loses even the design argument.

checklist.item: Remove every chance element from the paid path: no randomised question draw, no randomised opponent variance affecting payout, no loot-box or gacha reveal, no variable multiplier. Same question set, same order, same conditions for all entrants in a contest.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.cost: Engineering
checklist.prerequisite: Separate paid contest engine from the free duel engine
checklist.notes: This is what defeats the material-element states (N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1) 'Contest of chance' — CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(2), which is 'Gambling'; also AL, KY, MO, OH, OR, WA) and Tennessee's near-any-chance test (Tenn. Code s.39-17-501(1), 'to any degree contingent on chance'). FACT//DUEL's Expedition mechanic — staking points at three confidence tiers on rotating question sets — is the highest-risk surface here and must not carry real money.

checklist.item: Keep purchased coins structurally incapable of being staked. If a user buys coins, those coins must only ever be spent at a fixed price on a fixed item.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control
checklist.cost: Engineering
checklist.prerequisite: Two separate ledgers: purchased (spend-only) and earned (stakeable, worthless)
checklist.notes: Directly addresses Kater v. Churchill Downs, 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 2018) and RCW 9.46.0285, and the identical New York wording at Penal Law s.225.00(6) ('Something of value') — CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(1), which is 'Contest of chance'. Subdivision verified at nysenate.gov, 14 Sep 2026. A credit that extends the privilege of playing IS a thing of value; a staked-and-lost purchased coin is gambling in Washington with no cash-out at all.

[CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] ON HAWAII SPECIFICALLY: no Hawaii prize-promotion registration statute could be identified, and the claim sits badly next to the brief's own correct observation that Hawaii permits no legal gambling of any kind and has NO GAMING REGULATOR — there is no agency to register with. The operational danger is that a founder reads this line as meaning paid entry in Hawaii is curable by filing. IT IS NOT. GEOFENCE HAWAII. Do not attempt a Hawaii registration route without a primary cite from counsel. Verify the RI cite before relying on it too.

checklist.item: Do NOT rely on Arizona's amusement-gambling intellectual-contest registration as a route into Arizona.
checklist.issuer: Arizona Attorney General
checklist.cost: Fee UNVERIFIED

A cash-prize trivia contest cannot fit. Arizona is a geofence, not a registration.

checklist.item: Adopt an age gate — CORRECTED: not a flat 18+. Age of majority is 19 in Alabama and Nebraska and 21 in Mississippi, so use 18+ generally, 19+ in AL and NE, 21+ in MS, and 21+ in any state where the product could be characterised as gambling — with real identity verification on the paid path, not a self-declared date of birth.

checklist.cost: KYC vendor per-check fee (UNVERIFIED)
checklist.prerequisite: Accounts and server-side identity
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION] The brief prescribed a flat 18+ gate. Below the age of majority a minor can generally disaffirm the contract, which affects (a) enforceability of the terms of service and of the ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND CLASS-ACTION WAIVER the brief elsewhere tells the founder to build — the waiver is worth little against a user who can void the agreement — and (b) the minors' in-app-purchase exposure the brief correctly identifies as the most common consumer-protection enforcement hook against games. Current statutory cites for the AL/NE/MS majority ages are UNVERIFIED; confirm with counsel. Also a prerequisite for any MTL/BSA programme and for New Jersey's esports rule (participants 18+).

checklist.item: Automatic-renewal compliance for the subscription product: express affirmative consent, free-trial/free-to-pay-conversion disclosure, 7-30 day advance notice of fee changes, and same-medium (in-app) cancellation.
checklist.issuer: California AG and district attorneys; Virginia AG; New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
checklist.cost: Compliance/engineering only
checklist.leadTime: CA in force since 1 Jul 2025; VA 1 Jul 2026; NYC 1 Oct 2026
checklist.prerequisite: In-app cancel flow
checklist.notes: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code s.17600 et seq. as amended by A.B. 2863 (signed 24 Sep 2024). About 25 states have automatic-renewal laws; California, Virginia and NYC are the strictest. Selling via Apple/Google billing satisfies much of the cancellation mechanics but not the disclosure obligations.

checklist.item: Build the arbitration clause, class-action waiver and loss-recovery mitigation strategy BEFORE launch, because state gambling-loss-recovery statutes are the main private-litigation threat and they do not require a criminal conviction.
checklist.issuer: Private plaintiffs' bar (and, in Kentucky, 'any other person' after six months under KRS 372.040)
checklist.cost: Exposure is uncapped: Big Fish Casino settled Kater-line claims for $155m (secondary source, widely reported)
checklist.prerequisite: Terms of service and dispute-resolution design
checklist.notes: Verified live statutes: Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (recover losses of $50+ from the winner); Washington RCW 4.24.070. KENTUCKY — CORRECTED: the brief packed two sections into one number. KRS 372.020 is the LOSER'S OWN action to recover the amount lost ($5 or more). KRS 372.040 is the separate provision carrying the six-month window, the 'any other person' standing and TREBLE damages. Splitting them matters because s.372.040 is the provision that creates the outsized exposure. Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and Ohio have analogous statutes and were used in the 2026 prediction-market class actions against Kalshi, Robinhood and Webull (secondary: Illinois Answers Project, Mar 2026). [AUDIT ADDITION] Note the interaction with the age-gate item: an arbitration clause and class waiver do not reliably bind a user below the age of majority (19 in AL and NE, 21 in MS).

checklist.item: Confirm Apple App Store and Google Play real-money policy clearance before building the payment surface.
checklist.issuer: Apple; Google
checklist.cost: Store commission on any in-app purchase; nil for external real-money wallets where permitted
checklist.prerequisite: Evidence of licensure or a legal opinion, plus geo-restriction to permitted territories
checklist.notes: Both stores require real-money gaming apps to be geo-restricted to jurisdictions where the developer is licensed and to be submitted by the licensed entity. CORRECTED: the brief said 'no state licence exists for peer-to-peer trivia wagering'. Licences do exist in principle — Nevada NRS 463.160 licenses any game played for money with no skill/chance distinction, and New Jersey's DGE licenses esports event wagering — but none is available to this product at viable cost or lead time, so the practical conclusion is unchanged: MODEL B IS VERY LIKELY UNSHIPPABLE ON BOTH STORES. Policy citation UNVERIFIED — read the current guidelines directly before commissioning legal opinions.

checklist.item: Commission a per-state legal opinion from gaming counsel covering all 51 jurisdictions before the first real-money launch, and a separate money-transmission opinion.

checklist.cost: One published market data point: $15,000 for a 51-jurisdiction skill-gaming opinion (terms.law/Tokmakov advertised price). Full-service gaming firms will be materially more.
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec — counsel cannot opine on a moving design
checklist.notes: Walters Law Group's published position is that 'the only reliable way to evaluate the legality of a particular skill game in the United States is to engage experienced gaming counsel to render a legal opinion' and that any blanket list of legal states is unreliable. One firm reported reaching ZERO unconditionally cleared states in a recent comprehensive engagement. Treat this checklist as a map, not an opinion. [AUDIT ADDITION] The opinion scope must now also cover: (a) tribal compact exclusivity in CA, FL, OK and CT; (b) the money-transmission threshold question (transmission to another person) rather than assuming a 49-state programme; (c) player-side as distinct from operator-side liability; (d) unclaimed-property duties on unredeemed coin balances; and (e) whether an AMOE / free-entry structure opens any state that paid entry closes.

checklist.issuer: n/a
checklist.cost: Monitoring service or counsel retainer (UNVERIFIED)

Failed in 2026 but likely to return: Minnesota SF 4474/HF 4410; Florida SB 1580/HB 1467; Massachusetts H 4431; Mississippi SB 2104; Hawaii SB 3281; Texas SB 517; Arkansas SB 524. Active enforcement without legislation: Illinois Gaming Board issued 60+ cease-and-desist letters on 3 Mar 2026; Mississippi Gaming Commission C&Ds; New York AG Letitia James C&Ds to 26 platforms in Mar 2025; Kentucky AG litigation against VGW; Pennsylvania Supreme Court held in June 2026 that 'skill games' are slot machines under PA law.

checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED

Exclusivity provisions in state-tribal compacts in California, Florida, Oklahoma and Connecticut give tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming, and tribal objection has killed products that had a clean reading of the state criminal code. Oklahoma additionally grants tribal operators exclusive online gambling rights. This risk sits ALONGSIDE the statutes analysed in this lane, not inside them: clearing the penal code does not clear a compact objection. Specific compact provisions and their reach to a non-casino skill product are UNVERIFIED.

Several states treat unredeemed prepaid balances as abandoned property with reporting and remittance duties to the state. Whether closed-loop, non-redeemable game currency is exempt varies by state and is the specific question to ask. Thresholds, dormancy periods and exemptions per state: UNVERIFIED. The design consequence is concrete: build last-activity tracking and a balance-expiry/notice policy now rather than retrofitting it.

checklist.cost: Legal drafting

Several of the statutes it relies on reach the PERSON WHO PLAYS OR BETS, not just the house: 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('plays a game of chance or skill for money'), and Cal. Penal Code s.337a, which reaches making and ACCEPTING a bet. Illinois has a participant-side bona fide contest exception that does NOT shelter the operator; the mirror-image question — whether the operator's geofence leaves an individual user exposed — has to be answered too, because it drives the terms of service, the refund posture, and whether a balance must be returned to a user who played from a prohibited state. Per-state scope of player-side liability: UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Cost the free-entry / alternative-method-of-entry (AMOE) option before committing to Model C, and understand that it is the most legislatively targeted structure in the country right now.
checklist.issuer: n/a — design control, with counsel
checklist.cost: Engineering plus fulfilment of free entries; prize liability unchanged
checklist.prerequisite: A per-state opinion on whether removing consideration actually opens any state you care about
checklist.notes: The brief jumped from Model B to Model C without evaluating a genuine AMOE. A free entry of equal dignity (no purchase necessary, equal odds, equal prize eligibility, a real and usable free path) removes the CONSIDERATION element and can open states whose bar is consideration-based. It does NOT help where the statute does not turn on consideration in that way — Arizona, Florida, Delaware, South Dakota and Louisiana among them. And the decisive caution: THE ENTIRE 2025-26 DUAL-CURRENCY BAN WAVE CATALOGUED IN THIS LANE IS THE LEGISLATIVE RESPONSE TO EXACTLY THIS STRUCTURE — sweepstakes operators used an AMOE to argue they were not gambling, and ten states legislated against it. An AMOE is a legitimate option for a promotional contest; it is not a safe harbour in 2026. Which states it opens: UNVERIFIED.

As at 14 Sep 2026: NY (5 Dec 2025), CT and MT (1 Oct 2025), CA (1 Jan 2026) are in force; the IN, IA, ME, TN and LA dates are UNVERIFIED but all fall before today if correct; OKLAHOMA S.B. 1589 is the single listed prohibition still to come, effective 1 NOV 2026. DO NOT STAGE A LAUNCH INTO OKLAHOMA IN THE SEVEN-WEEK WINDOW. The conduct becomes a Class C2 felony with no wind-down, the definitions are the broadest of the 2026 wave, liability extends to your payment and geolocation vendors, and Oklahoma also has tribal exclusivity over online gambling. Ship the geofence with Oklahoma already blocked and a per-state effective-date column so the next wave is a config change.

subdivisions.name: Alabama
subdivisions.detail: Material-element test: a 'contest of chance' is one whose outcome 'depends in a material degree upon an element of chance, notwithstanding that skill of the contestants may also be a factor'. A skill-dominant trivia contest with no randomisation is defensible (Model C); Model B is unsettled and exposed to Alabama's gambling-loss-recovery statute, which was used in the 2026 prediction-market class actions. No sweepstakes ban enacted. Constitutional ban on lotteries (Ala. Const. art. IV s.65) is a background risk for anything pot-like. [AUDIT ADDITION] AGE OF MAJORITY IN ALABAMA IS 19, not 18. A flat 18+ gate leaves 18-year-old Alabama users able to disaffirm the contract, which undermines the terms of service, the arbitration clause and the class-action waiver against them, and sharpens the minors' in-app-purchase exposure. Statutory cite UNVERIFIED.
subdivisions.authority: Ala. Code s.13A-12-20(4) ('contest of chance'), s.13A-12-21 (simple gambling) — text via FindLaw secondary. Alabama loss-recovery statute section UNVERIFIED.

subdivisions.name: Alaska
subdivisions.detail: Gambling is defined by reference to a contest of chance or a future contingent event not under the participant's control; no enacted sweepstakes ban and no express skill-wagering prohibition found. Model C plausibly permitted, Model B unsettled. Alaska has no commercial gaming regime, so there is no licence to obtain.
subdivisions.authority: AS 11.66.280 (gambling definitions) — section text UNVERIFIED in this pass.

subdivisions.name: Arizona
subdivisions.detail: THE CLEAREST PROHIBITION IN THE COUNTRY. 'Gambling' expressly includes 'one act of risking or giving something of value for the opportunity to obtain a benefit from a game or contest of chance OR SKILL'. The skill/chance debate is legislated away. The only exceptions are 'amusement gambling' — merchandise prizes under $10 wholesale, coupons capped at $550 aggregate, or an intellectual contest where the payment is part of an established purchase price with no increment added. A cash-prize trivia duel or paid-entry contest fits none of them. A.R.S. s.13-3311 provides an AG registration route for amusement-gambling intellectual contests but only inside those prize caps. Geofence. Models A and D unaffected.
subdivisions.authority: A.R.S. s.13-3301(4) (definition of 'gambling'), s.13-3301 (amusement gambling), s.13-3311 (registration, filing of rules, sworn statement, exceptions) — current Arizona Revised Statutes, azleg.gov.

subdivisions.name: Arkansas
subdivisions.detail: Broad gaming-device prohibition reaching any device 'at which any money or property may be won or lost', with no chance element required. Narrow safe harbour: paid ESPORTS tournaments are expressly not gambling if entry fees are paid in cash, prizes are disclosed in advance, and outcomes reflect the skill and performance of competitors (eff. 31 Jul 2023). A mobile trivia app is very unlikely to be an 'esports tournament' as defined. Geofence unless counsel can bring the product inside ch. 23-118. Blocked by Skillz.
subdivisions.authority: Ark. Code s.5-66-104 (gaming devices — prohibition); Ark. Code ss.23-118-101 to 23-118-103 (Paid Esports Tournaments, HB 1349 of 2023, eff. 31 Jul 2023).

subdivisions.name: California
subdivisions.detail: TWO SEPARATE PROHIBITIONS. (1) Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) criminalises laying, making, offering or accepting any bet 'upon the result, or purported result, of any trial ... or contest ... of skill, speed or power of endurance of person or animal, OR BETWEEN PERSONS' — a player-v-player trivia stake is squarely within it; subdivisions (2), (3) and (4) reach operating a place for such wagers, RECEIVING OR HOLDING the money staked, and recording the wagers. First offence up to one year and/or $5,000. (2) Penal Code s.337o (added by AB 831, signed 11 Oct 2025, eff. 1 Jan 2026) bans operating an 'online sweepstakes game' — a dual-currency internet game that simulates gambling and awards cash or cash equivalents — and extends liability to financial institutions, payment processors, geolocation providers, content suppliers and media affiliates who knowingly and willfully support it; misdemeanour, $1,000-$25,000 per violation, up to one year. A trivia duel arguably does not 'simulate gambling' for s.337o purposes, but s.337a(a)(6) closes that gap. California applies the predominance test generally (In re Allen, 59 Cal.2d 5 (1962)), so Model C with an operator-funded fixed prize and no player-v-player pot is the only structure with a case — get a California opinion. [AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL COMPACT EXPOSURE: state-tribal compact exclusivity gives tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming here, separate from the criminal code. Clearing the penal analysis does not clear a compact objection. Compact provisions UNVERIFIED. California's tribal exclusivity is among the most consequential in the country. [AUDIT ADDITION] PLAYER-SIDE LIABILITY: Cal. Penal Code s.337a reaches MAKING and ACCEPTING a bet, not only operating a place or holding stakes, so the individual player is within the statute too. Scope UNVERIFIED; put it to California counsel.
subdivisions.authority: Cal. Penal Code s.337a(a)(2),(3),(4),(6); Cal. Penal Code s.337o (AB 831, eff. 1 Jan 2026); Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code s.17539.1 (as amended by AB 831). Regulator: California Attorney General / Department of Justice Bureau of Gambling Control.

subdivisions.name: Colorado
subdivisions.detail: Colorado's gambling definition is generally understood to exclude 'bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries', which would support Model C and possibly Model B. But promotions-law compliance guides list Colorado as a state that does not permit entry fees in contests. The two framings conflict and I could not resolve them from a primary source in this pass. No sweepstakes ban enacted. Treat as unresolved and get a Colorado opinion before taking paid entries.
subdivisions.authority: C.R.S. s.18-10-102 (gambling definitions) — skill-contest exclusion text UNVERIFIED. Conflicting secondary source: Sweeppea state compliance guide.

subdivisions.name: Connecticut
subdivisions.detail: Cuts both ways, so treat it as prohibited. The gambling definition DOES exclude 'legal contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' (verbatim), which on its face supports Model C and even Model B. But S.B. 1235 / Public Act 25-112 (signed 11 Jun 2025, eff. 1 Oct 2025) makes operating an online sweepstakes casino a CLASS D FELONY, and the entire real-money skill industry (including Skillz) blocks Connecticut, which tells you how the Department of Consumer Protection reads the 'legal contests' circularity. Geofence unless you are willing to fund a test case. [AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL COMPACT EXPOSURE: state-tribal compact exclusivity gives tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming here, separate from the criminal code. Clearing the penal analysis does not clear a compact objection. Compact provisions UNVERIFIED.
subdivisions.authority: Conn. Gen. Stat. s.53-278a(2) (definition of 'gambling', skill-contest exclusion, 2024 revision in force); Conn. Public Act 25-112 (S.B. 1235), eff. 1 Oct 2025. Regulator: Department of Consumer Protection, Gaming Division.

subdivisions.name: Delaware
subdivisions.detail: Constitutional ban: all forms of gambling are prohibited except state-controlled lotteries, s.17B lotteries, pari-mutuel horse wagering and bingo. Separately, 'advancing gambling in the first degree' covers keeping or using any book, device or apparatus for receiving, recording or registering 'bets or wagers upon the result of any trial or contest of SKILL, speed or power of endurance of human or beast' — the 19th-century formula that catches player-v-player skill wagering explicitly. Class A misdemeanour. Blocked by Skillz. Geofence.
subdivisions.authority: Del. Const. art. II s.17 (Lotteries and Other Gambling); 11 Del. C. s.1403 (advancing gambling in the first degree); 11 Del. C. s.1401 (second degree); 11 Del. C. s.1432 (gambling definitions).

subdivisions.name: District of Columbia
subdivisions.detail: No express skill-wagering prohibition identified and no enacted sweepstakes ban, but B26-0656 (Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, introduced 9 Apr 2026, under Council review as of mid-2026) would legalise regulated online gaming while banning sweepstakes casinos. DC's sporting-event definition treats esports as games of skill, which is mildly helpful for Model C. Operator-level restrictions and scrutiny already reported. Monitor closely — DC could flip within one Council period.
subdivisions.authority: D.C. Code s.22-1701 et seq. (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED; D.C. Code s.36-601.01 (sporting events, esports as skill) via secondary source; DC Council B26-0656 (pending).

subdivisions.name: Florida
subdivisions.detail: Fla. Stat. s.849.14 is titled 'Unlawful to bet on result of trial or contest of skill, speed or power or endurance' and makes it a second-degree misdemeanour (up to 60 days, $500) to stake, bet or wager any money or thing of value on such a result. The legislature had to enact a SPECIFIC carve-out for bowling tournaments with entry fees and a purse (s.849.141), which demonstrates that entry-fee-funded prizes would otherwise be caught. Separately, s.849.094 requires filing rules and prize lists with FDACS at least 7 days out and a trust account or bond where total prize value exceeds $5,000. Florida also has no explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. 2026 sweepstakes bills SB 1580 and HB 1467 both died. Geofence for paid play. [AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL COMPACT EXPOSURE: state-tribal compact exclusivity gives tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming here, separate from the criminal code. Clearing the penal analysis does not clear a compact objection. Compact provisions UNVERIFIED. Florida's compact with the Seminole Tribe is broad and actively enforced.
subdivisions.authority: Fla. Stat. s.849.14 (in force, 2025 Florida Statutes); Fla. Stat. s.849.141 (bowling exception); Fla. Stat. s.849.094 (game promotions). Regulators: Florida Attorney General; Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Florida Gaming Control Commission.

subdivisions.name: Georgia
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering statute, but Georgia's gambling-loss-recovery statute is live and was used in the 2026 wave of class actions against prediction-market operators and their brokers. Georgia also has an aggressive history on 'coin-operated amusement machines' with no-cash-prize rules. Model C plausibly defensible under a predominance analysis; Model B carries real private-litigation risk independent of any prosecution.
subdivisions.authority: O.C.G.A. s.16-12-21 (gambling) and s.16-12-35 (bona fide skill contest / amusement machine rules) — section text UNVERIFIED; O.C.G.A. s.13-8-3 (gambling contracts void; recovery) cited in 2026 class actions (secondary: Illinois Answers Project, Mar 2026).

subdivisions.name: Hawaii
subdivisions.detail: Hawaii has NO legal gambling of any kind — no lottery, no casinos, no sports betting — and its gambling offence tracks the model-penal-code 'contest of chance or a future contingent event not under his control' formula. SB 3281 (2026), which would have criminalised promoting illegal electronic gambling, was deferred. [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] The brief reported, from promotions-law compliance guides only, that contests requiring an entry fee with prizes of $5,000 or more must be registered and bonded in Hawaii. THE AUDIT RECOMMENDS STRIKING THAT LINE: no Hawaii prize-promotion registration statute is identifiable, and it sits badly against the fact — which the brief itself states correctly — that Hawaii has no legal gambling and NO GAMING REGULATOR, so there is no agency to register with. It is retained here only as a contested claim, flagged. THE OPERATIONAL POINT IS UNAMBIGUOUS EITHER WAY: GEOFENCE HAWAII for any paid stake. Do not treat paid entry in Hawaii as curable by filing a registration; the AG has no tolerance and there is no licensing route.
subdivisions.authority: HRS s.712-1220 (gambling definitions) and s.712-1223 (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED; [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] Hawaii contest registration/bonding threshold from secondary promotions-law sources only, no primary statute located — audit recommends striking it.

subdivisions.name: Idaho
subdivisions.detail: The Idaho Constitution bans gambling broadly and expressly prohibits 'any electronic or electromechanical imitation or simulation of any form of casino gambling'. Sweepstakes-industry trackers list Idaho alongside Washington as a state where pre-existing constitutional and statutory law already prohibits the dual-currency model without new legislation. Idaho's statutory gambling definition follows the contest-of-chance formula. Geofence Model B; Model C needs an Idaho opinion.
subdivisions.authority: Idaho Const. art. III s.20 (gambling prohibited, including simulations of casino gambling); Idaho Code s.18-3801 (gambling defined) — subsection detail UNVERIFIED.

subdivisions.name: Illinois
subdivisions.detail: Illinois criminalises playing 'a game of chance OR SKILL for money or other thing of value' — the statute names skill expressly. There is a participant-side exception for a bona fide contest for the determination of skill, speed, strength or endurance where awards are made only to entrants, but it does not shelter the OPERATOR, who remains exposed under the keeping-a-gambling-place and operating provisions. Illinois also has the most usable loss-recovery statute in the country: anyone who loses $50 or more by gambling may sue the winner in the circuit court. The Illinois Gaming Board issued cease-and-desist letters to 60+ sweepstakes operators on 3 Mar 2026. Geofence Model B; Model C needs an Illinois opinion focused on operator liability. [AUDIT ADDITION] PLAYER-SIDE LIABILITY: 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) reaches the person who PLAYS, and the bona fide contest exception at 5/28-1(b)(2) is participant-side. So in Illinois the geofence protects the company from the operator-side offence while an Illinois user who plays is separately exposed — which drives the terms of service and the return-of-balance posture, not just the block list.
subdivisions.authority: 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('plays a game of chance or skill for money'); 720 ILCS 5/28-1(b)(2) (bona fide contest exception, participant-side); 720 ILCS 5/28-3 (keeping a gambling place); 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (loss recovery, $50 threshold). Regulator: Illinois Gaming Board; Illinois Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Indiana
subdivisions.detail: [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] DATES UNVERIFIED FROM A PRIMARY SOURCE. H.B. 1052, reported signed 12 Mar 2026 as Public Law 153-2026, prohibits online sweepstakes games built on dual- or multi-currency systems that simulate lottery games or casino-style gaming, reported effective 1 Jul 2026, with civil fines up to $100,000 per violation. The Indiana General Assembly source could not be reached to confirm the signing date, effective date or penalty figure — confirm from the enrolled act before these enter a launch timeline. Substance is otherwise consistent with the 2026 wave. Operators reportedly exited the state in July 2026. Skillz separately restricts real-prize play in Indiana where playing cards are involved. A trivia duel may fall outside 'simulates lottery or casino-style gaming', but the Indiana Gaming Commission now has a fresh enforcement mandate. Geofence Model B.

subdivisions.name: Iowa
subdivisions.detail: CORRECTED CHARACTERISATION: Iowa is NOT one of the express dual-currency sweepstakes bans and must not be counted as one. S.F. 2289 (reported signed by Gov. Reynolds 15 May 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026 — [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] both dates UNVERIFIED from a primary legislative source) expands the Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission's enforcement authority and expressly authorises cease-and-desist orders against operators offering games of chance, sports wagering, gambling OR SWEEPSTAKES GAMING in Iowa without a licence. As the brief itself noted, it does NOT define dual-currency systems and does NOT create a new criminal offence — it is a broad enforcement grant. That makes it MORE dangerous for a novel product than a narrow casino-simulation ban, because the Commission decides what counts and there is no definitional element to argue against; but it is a different compliance question from CA, NY or OK, and the brief's headline count of twelve bans conflated the two. Iowa Code ch. 99B restricts games between individuals to bona fide social relationships. Real-money skill apps block Iowa. Geofence.

subdivisions.name: Kansas
subdivisions.detail: Kansas defines a 'bet' by reference to chance, with a bona fide business transaction exclusion. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Kansas historically treated daily fantasy sports as requiring legislative authorisation, which signals a restrictive AG posture toward novel paid-entry contests. Model C plausibly defensible; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: K.S.A. s.21-6403 (definitions of 'bet' and 'gambling') — section text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Kansas Racing and Gaming Commission; Kansas Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Kentucky
subdivisions.detail: HIGHEST PRIVATE-LITIGATION RISK IN THE UNITED STATES even though there is no sweepstakes ban. CORRECTED — THE CITE IS TWO SECTIONS, NOT ONE. KRS 372.020 is the LOSER'S OWN action: a person who loses $5 or more in a 24-hour period through illegal gambling may sue to recover the amount lost. KRS 372.040 is the SEPARATE provision that carries the six-month window, the 'ANY OTHER PERSON' standing and TREBLE damages — if the loser does not sue within six months, any other person may sue for treble the value of the loss. The brief packed both into 'KRS 372.020'. The split matters because s.372.040 is the provision that actually creates the outsized exposure: it converts a private remedy into a bounty available to strangers and litigation funders. Kentucky used this machinery to obtain a nine-figure judgment against PokerStars and the AG has active litigation against VGW. Kentucky's gambling definition uses the material-degree test, with a reported exception where results are determined solely by skill and prizes are predetermined — which, if correct, is a precise fit for Model C and a precise mismatch for Model B. Kentucky was also a venue in the 2026 prediction-market class actions. Model C: arguable. Model B: do not.

Regulator: Kentucky Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Louisiana
subdivisions.detail: Louisiana's gambling statute has NO CHANCE ELEMENT AT ALL: gambling is 'the intentional conducting, or directly assisting in the conducting, as a business, of any game, contest, lottery, or contrivance whereby a person risks the loss of anything of value in order to realize a profit'. That definition catches a paid-entry skill contest run as a business on its face. On top of that, H.B. 53 (Act 48) and H.B. 883 (Act 182), signed 25 May 2026 and effective 1 Aug 2026, ban dual-currency online sweepstakes, treat them as 'gambling by computer', raise the maximum fine for illegal online gambling operations from $20,000 to $100,000 with up to five years, and bring racketeering exposure. Absolute geofence.

subdivisions.name: Maryland
subdivisions.detail: Maryland has a narrow express carve-out for ESPORTS — competitions involving video games (first-person shooters, real-time strategy, MOBAs) where players compete against each other and 'the dominant element determining the results is the relative skill of the players' — with the Comptroller empowered to adopt regulations. A trivia app is not obviously within the listed genres. Maryland's general gambling provisions reach keeping or having an interest in a gaming device or place used for gambling (6 months to 1 year, $500). Promotions-law guides report that Maryland does not permit consideration in skill contests. Three 2026 sweepstakes bills (HB 1226, HB 295, SB 652) were introduced; none enacted. Unresolved — get a Maryland opinion, and consider whether the product can be characterised as an esport under s.12-114.

subdivisions.name: Massachusetts
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban (H 4431, which would have legalised iGaming and banned sweepstakes, failed in the 2026 session). Massachusetts has an active AG with promulgated daily-fantasy-sports regulations, which is a useful signal that paid-entry skill contests are regulable rather than per se unlawful — but also that the AG expects to regulate them. Massachusetts was a venue in the 2026 prediction-market loss-recovery class actions. Some real-money skill apps block Massachusetts. Model C: arguable with counsel; Model B: unsettled and litigated.

subdivisions.name: Michigan
subdivisions.detail: Michigan's gambling provisions are generally understood to reach betting on the result of 'any contest of skill, speed or power of endurance of man or beast', the same 19th-century formula that appears in California, Florida and Delaware — but I could not verify the Michigan text in this pass. Michigan has a fully built iGaming regulator (MGCB) which has been active against unlicensed operators. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Treat as unresolved and verify MCL s.750.301 before taking paid stakes.

subdivisions.name: Minnesota
subdivisions.detail: Minnesota's 'bet' definition is chance-based and is generally understood to exclude 'a contest of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' — which would support both Model C and, on its face, Model B. Promotions guides nonetheless treat Minnesota cautiously. The 2026 sweepstakes bans (SF 4474 / HF 4410) failed when the session ended 18 May 2026 and will likely return. Separately relevant to Model A: Minnesota's virtual-currency customer disclosure rules under Minn. Stat. s.53B.72 took effect 1 Jan 2026.

subdivisions.name: Mississippi
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban — SB 2104 died in committee in 2026 — but the Mississippi Gaming Commission has issued cease-and-desist letters to sweepstakes casinos and unlicensed online operators. Mississippi's general gambling statutes are broad and the state has a full casino regulator with an enforcement appetite. Model B: geofence. Model C: Mississippi opinion needed. [AUDIT ADDITION] AGE OF MAJORITY IN MISSISSIPPI IS 21, not 18 — the widest gap in the country, affecting contract enforceability, the arbitration clause and class-action waiver, and in-app-purchase exposure for every user aged 18 to 20. subdivisions.name: Montana
subdivisions.status: prohibited for Model B (S.B. 555); UNRESOLVED for Model C — corrected
subdivisions.detail: CORRECTED — THE BRIEF'S PRIMARY MONTANA CLAIM IS WITHDRAWN. The brief said Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 defines a lawful 'contest of skill' as one in which skill predominates AND 'the contestant is not required to pay anything of value or purchase anything in order to participate', and used that to make Montana an absolute geofence with 'TWO INDEPENDENT PROHIBITIONS'. Verified directly at mca.legmt.gov on 14 Sep 2026: (a) s.23-5-110 is titled 'Public policy of state concerning gambling' — it is a legislative-findings and licensing-privilege section, it defines no terms and contains no paid-entry disqualifier; (b) the definitions section is s.23-5-112, which defines 44 terms and 'contest of skill' IS NOT AMONG THEM (the list runs Antique gambling device, Applicant, Application, Associated gambling business, Authorized equipment, Bingo ... through Video gambling machine); (c) s.23-5-112(14)(a) defines gambling as 'risking any money, credit, deposit, check, property, or other thing of value for a gain that is contingent in whole or in part upon lot, chance, or the operation of a gambling device or gambling enterprise' — a CHANCE-BASED definition that cuts AGAINST the brief's reading, not for it. A 'contest of skill' definition with a paid-entry bar is repeated in several promotions-law guides for Montana but NO PRIMARY CITATION COULD BE LOCATED: treat it as UNVERIFIED and do not rely on it. CONSEQUENCE: Montana comes OUT of the list of states that criminalise wagering on contests of skill by statute. WHAT STILL STANDS: S.B. 555, effective 1 Oct 2025, amended Title 23 ch. 5 to add a definition of 'online sweepstakes gambling' capturing the dual-currency model — reportedly the first dedicated dual-currency ban in the country — with felony penalties. MODEL B: geofence Montana on S.B. 555. MODEL C: now UNRESOLVED rather than absolutely barred — a paid-entry, operator-funded, fixed-prize knowledge contest with randomisation stripped from the paid path has a real argument under the chance-based s.23-5-112(14)(a), and a Montana opinion could remove Montana from the Model C block list. Keep it geofenced until that opinion exists. Footnote: Montana is the only state with no money transmitter licence requirement.

Code Ann. s.23-5-110 ('Public policy of state concerning gambling' — verified 14 Sep 2026 at mca.legmt.gov; the brief's 'contest of skill' cite to this section is WITHDRAWN); Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-112 (Definitions — 44 defined terms, no 'contest of skill'; gambling defined at (14)(a), chance-based, verified verbatim 14 Sep 2026); Mont. S.B. 555 (2025), eff. 1 Oct 2025, amending Mont. Code Ann. tit. 23 ch. 5. Regulator: Montana Department of Justice, Gambling Control Division.

subdivisions.detail: Nebraska's constitution restricts games of chance and the statutory gambling definition turns on an element of chance. Promotions-law compliance guides list Nebraska among states that do not permit entry fees in contests. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Unresolved — verify with a Nebraska opinion before taking paid entries. [AUDIT ADDITION] AGE OF MAJORITY IN NEBRASKA IS 19, not 18 — same contract-enforceability and arbitration-clause consequence as Alabama. Statutory cite UNVERIFIED.

subdivisions.name: Nevada
subdivisions.detail: PRACTICALLY PROHIBITED, BUT A LICENSED PATH DOES EXIST IN PRINCIPLE. 'Game' or 'gambling game' means any game played with cards, dice, equipment or any mechanical or electronic device or machine FOR MONEY, property, checks, credit or any representative of value — the statute draws NO distinction between games of skill and games of chance. Any game that lets a player walk away with real value is a gambling game requiring a full Nevada gaming licence under NRS 463.160. CORRECTED: the brief elsewhere asserted that 'no state licenses this' and that 'lawful-only-with-licence is not available as an answer'. That is contradicted by this very entry. NRS 463.160 IS a licensed path — it is simply prohibitive: a Nevada non-restricted licence is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar suitability process with no product-appropriate category for a peer-to-peer mobile trivia app. The accurate statement is 'no off-the-shelf licence category at viable cost and lead time', not 'no licence exists'. The Gaming Control Board does not recognise the dual-currency sweepstakes model as exempt. S.B. 256 (2025) added ENFORCEMENT TOOLS against unlicensed online operators including freezing earnings — CORRECTED: it is NOT an express dual-currency ban and must not be counted as one; the Nevada question turns on Board discretion, not on a statutory dual-currency definition you can read against the product. Geofence.
subdivisions.authority: NRS s.463.0152 ('Game' and 'gambling game' defined); NRS s.463.160 (licence required — a real, if commercially unavailable, licensed path); Nev. S.B. 256 (2025) — enforcement-authority grant, not an express dual-currency ban. Regulator: Nevada Gaming Control Board; Nevada Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: New Hampshire
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering prohibition. New Hampshire has an express fantasy-sports statute, which signals that paid-entry skill contests are regulable rather than per se criminal. Model C plausibly defensible; Model B unsettled.

subdivisions.name: New Jersey
subdivisions.detail: Mixed, but treat Model B as prohibited. NEW JERSEY IS HELPFUL FOR MODEL C: N.J.S.A. 5:19-1 is titled 'Participation in contests of skill not deemed unlawful gambling', and New Jersey has a mature Division of Gaming Enforcement that regulates esports event wagering (participants must be 18+). CORRECTED, RELEVANT TO THE HEADLINE: the DGE's esports event wagering licence is one of the two counter-examples to the brief's claim that 'no state licenses this' — licensure exists in principle, it just does not fit a peer-to-peer trivia app at viable cost. [CONTESTED — audit flagged at "possible" confidence] A5447 is reported signed 15 Aug 2025 and bans most dual-currency online sweepstakes with enforcement mechanisms; its TEXT is confirmed to exist and to carry civil penalties of $100,000 first offence / $250,000 subsequent, but its ENACTMENT and the 15 Aug 2025 signing date could NOT be confirmed (NJ Legislature and LegiScan blocked). Confirm before relying. New Jersey is also one of the eight states reported to have NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption, so the custody question is harder here. Model B: geofence. Model C: New Jersey is one of the better states, with a DGE opinion. [AUDIT ADDITION] TRIBAL COMPACT EXPOSURE: state-tribal compact exclusivity gives tribes independent standing and enforcement leverage against unlicensed real-money gaming here, separate from the criminal code. Clearing the penal analysis does not clear a compact objection. Compact provisions UNVERIFIED.

(gambling offences); NJ DGE esports event wagering rules (a real licensed category). Regulator: New Jersey Division of Gaming Enforcement; Casino Control Commission.

subdivisions.name: New York
subdivisions.detail: THE MOST IMPORTANT STATE TO GET RIGHT, AND THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE. (1) MODEL B IS BANNED OUTRIGHT: Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law s.912 (added by S5935A, ch. 605 of 2025, signed by Gov. Hochul 5 Dec 2025, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY WITH NO WIND-DOWN) prohibits dual-currency online sweepstakes platforms that let players exchange game currency for cash prizes or cash equivalents and that mimic casino gaming, sports betting, lottery products or bingo — and reaches technology and game suppliers, platform providers, PAYMENT PROCESSORS AND FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, geolocation firms and MEDIA AFFILIATES. $10,000-$100,000 per violation plus licence revocation or ineligibility. AG Letitia James had already sent cease-and-desist letters to 26 platforms in March 2025. (2) MODEL A HAS A TRAP — CITATION CORRECTED: N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(6), 'Something of value', includes 'any form of credit or promise' involving 'extension of a service, entertainment or a PRIVILEGE OF PLAYING AT A GAME OR SCHEME WITHOUT CHARGE' — the same wording the Ninth Circuit relied on in Kater under Washington law. The brief cited this to s.225.00(1), which is wrong. Verified subdivision-by-subdivision at nysenate.gov on 14 Sep 2026: (1) 'Contest of chance', (2) 'Gambling', (3) 'Player', (4) 'Advance gambling activity', (5) 'Profit from gambling activity', (6) 'Something of value', (7) 'Gambling device', (8) 'Slot machine', (9) 'Bookmaking', (10) 'Lottery', (11) 'Policy or the numbers game', (12) 'Unlawful'. THE SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS IS UNCHANGED: a purchased coin that is staked and lost is a thing of value in New York even with no cash-out. (3) MODEL C — MATERIALLY QUALIFIED. The brief called White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (2022) 'THE BEST AUTHORITY IN THE COUNTRY' and said 'Build to that sentence.' That is overstated and the overstatement is operationally dangerous. White v. Cuomo was a holding on Article I s.9 of the NEW YORK CONSTITUTION, concerning interactive fantasy sports contests that the legislature had AFFIRMATIVELY AUTHORIZED in Racing Law article 14 and expressly exempted from Penal Law article 225; the court held that ample support existed for the legislature's determination that those authorized contests were lawful skill-based competitions. It does NOT hold that an UNAUTHORIZED paid-entry trivia contest escapes the material-degree contest-of-chance test at Penal Law s.225.00(1), and it has no precedential force in any other state. The reported 4-3 split is UNVERIFIED — a secondary source describes a DiFiore majority and a Wilson dissent joined by two judges, consistent with 4-3 but not confirmed from the opinion; do not state the split. WHAT SURVIVES AND IS WORTH KEEPING: the three attributes the Court treated as characteristic of lawful skill competition — substantial player influence, predetermined fixed prizes, a neutral operator — are a sound DESIGN TARGET that Model C meets and Model B does not. Treat them as a design heuristic with New York constitutional support, not as clearance, and get a New York penal-code opinion separately. (4) Note the material-degree test at Penal Law s.225.00(1) (CORRECTED from the brief's s.225.00(2), which is 'Gambling') and the GBL art. 24-A s.369-e registration and bond for prize pools over $5,000 (30 days' notice, $100 fee, bond equal to total prize value — figures from law-firm guides, UNVERIFIED).

Penal Law s.225.00(1) ('Contest of chance', material degree) and s.225.00(6) ('Something of value') — CORRECTED numbering, verified at nysenate.gov 14 Sep 2026; N.Y. Penal Law s.225.05 (promoting gambling 2d); White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (N.Y. 2022) — NY Const. art. I s.9 only, IFS authorized by Racing Law art. 14 and exempted from Penal Law art. 225, vote split UNVERIFIED; N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law art. 24-A s.369-e. Regulators: New York State Gaming Commission; New York Attorney General; New York Department of State.
